name: Mamluk Sultanate

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 2.1 million km2 for 1260-1348 (high, includes desert margins). No 1260 polygon exists: world_1200 still shows the Ayyubids, so the later world_1279 Mamluke Sultanate polygon is used; it measures 1.24 million km2 (mid). Low reflects that northern Syria was only won after Ain Jalut (September 1260).

population.note: Seshat codes 5-6 million for 1260-1348 and notes ~6-7 million at the 14th-century peak. HYDE/OWID Egypt 1200-1300 = 4.0-4.7 million plus Syria-Palestine ~1.5-2 million.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Cairo 200,000-500,000 (Seshat), Alexandria, Damascus, Aleppo.

activePersonnel.note: Mamluk army at Ain Jalut 15,000-20,000 (Nicolle 1990 p. 116; Waterson 2007 p. 75), including Ayyubid Syrian refugees and Khwarazmians. Baybars later expanded the army from 10,000 cavalry to 40,000 (Asbridge 2010, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate), so ~10,000 regular cavalry is the low.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Bedouin tribes, Turkmen and Kurdish auxiliaries and the troops of Syrian Ayyubid princes who submitted after Ain Jalut.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Naffatun, armourers, siege engineers and the few galley crews.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Military service was the preserve of the imported mamluk caste and halqa; the Egyptian peasantry was not levied.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Royal mamluks and the mamluks of the amirs, armoured horse archers who also charged with lance; part of the ~10,000 cavalry of 1260 (Asbridge, via the article).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: lamellar and mail, composite bow, lance, the best horses of the region.

training.note: Rubric 1.0: furusiyya training from boyhood in the barracks schools.

count.note: Educated guess. Halqa, Khwarazmian and Bedouin light horse.
Educated guess. Garrison and citadel infantry.
Educated guess. Foot archers and naffatun with incendiaries.
Educated guess. Counterweight and traction trebuchets in the citadels; the great siege trains came under Baybars and Qalawun.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Islamic counterweight trebuchets among the era's best.

count.note: Educated guess. A small Nile and coastal galley force; Baybars' 1271 fleet of ~17 galleys (11 lost off Cyprus) came later.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: Qutuz and Baybars lured Kitbuqa's tumen into the Ain Jalut valley with a feigned retreat and won.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.75 minus: khushdashiyya bonds within each mamluk household, but factional: Baybars killed Qutuz weeks after Ain Jalut.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: existential defence against the Mongols, crowned by victory.

weapons.note: Anchor 4 (1250): composite bow, lance, counterweight trebuchet, incendiaries.

armor.note: Anchor 4: lamellar and mail, horse armour for the elite.

ships.note: Anchor 3: a few galleys; the Mamluks were a land power.

fortification.note: Anchor 4: Cairo Citadel, Damascus and Aleppo citadels.

logistics.note: Anchor 4: Nile transport, granaries, camel trains across Sinai.

communications.note: Anchor 4 minus in 1260: the barid with relay horses and pigeon post was rebuilt by Baybars in the 1260s.

isr.note: Anchor 4: scouting and Syrian informants tracked Kitbuqa.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Most land revenue was assigned as iqta to mamluks and halqa; the state was built to pay its army.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Textiles, sugar refining, metalwork in Cairo and Damascus.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Nile irrigation agriculture with high yields.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; medieval age structures were similar (high mortality, young population).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Caravan and barid routes Cairo-Gaza-Damascus-Aleppo; little engineered road.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Alexandria, Damietta, Rosetta, Gaza; most Levantine ports still Frankish.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Nile and Red Sea shipping; Mediterranean trade carried by Italians.

supplyRangeKm.note: Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1) scaled up for camel trains across the Sinai and Syrian desert.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Camels, horses, donkeys and buffalo.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: fortified Cairo behind the Sinai desert, whose heat and lack of pasture punish steppe armies.

notes: Snapshot = September 1260, the Ain Jalut campaign, Qutuz sultan (killed by Baybars in October). The mamluks and halqa were salaried standing professionals paid through iqta, so they are activePersonnel; Bedouin and Syrian allies are reserves. Amitai-Preiss (Mongols and Mamluks, 1995) argues the two armies at Ain Jalut were roughly equal, Kitbuqa having 10,000-12,000 (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ain_Jalut). Population convention: Egypt plus the Syria and Palestine won in 1260; Frankish coastal states, Kerak (Ayyubid until 1263) and Lesser Armenia excluded. No 1260 polygon exists; see the territory note.
